# Left-quantile convex obstacle for actual buffered-depth sublevels

This is a fixed-body scalar theorem. It packages the exact CLOSED depth
sublevel constraint as an upper obstacle for a positive full-space parameter.
It retains every ambient oblique cap and every pure-base cap. It proves no
Gamma estimate or new global mixed centerpoint bound.

The archived source
`candidate 8fda4210ff6d4aaf`
already proves a projected convex threshold for depth SUPERLEVELS. The new
obstacle uses the OTHER endpoint of a quantile plateau and works at each mark,
before projecting in the continuous coordinate. The atomic domain and boundary
conventions are consequently different; they must not be interchanged.

## 1. Actual setting and the two quantile endpoints

Let P be a finite complete base and K_p positive full-dimensional convex
 d-fibers, d>=1, of an actual compatible canonical hull C. Write

    mu=sum_p dX|K_p,     M=mu(S),     0<Q<M,
    Gamma(u) a fixed norm on continuous covectors.

The within-fiber covariance norm is an allowed choice. For a real base
z in conv(P), let C_z denote the actual real fiber of C. Every such fiber is
full dimensional. Let b_base(z) be the weighted CLOSED pure-base depth at z.
All continuous covectors below satisfy Gamma(u)=1, so u is nonzero and ranges
over a compact set.

For N=(a,u), put F_N(c)=mu{a.Z+u.X>=c}. Since every sampled fiber is full
dimensional and u!=0, this is a continuous nonincreasing tail with limits M
and zero. Its Q-level may be a nontrivial closed interval. Define

    c_Q^-(a,u)=min{c:F_N(c)<=Q},
    c_Q^+(a,u)=max{c:F_N(c)>=Q}.                       (1)

Both endpoints are finite, the tail equals Q at them, and

    F_N(c)<=Q iff c>=c_Q^-,
    F_N(c)>=Q iff c<=c_Q^+.

The sublevel theorem needs c_Q^-, not the archived c_Q^+. For instance two
unit-length projection intervals separated by a gap have constant tail on
that gap; replacing one endpoint by the other changes an equality constraint.
No strict quantile convention removes that distinction.

## 2. A finite status-clamping lemma

Fix a real source (z,y) and a bounded interval of displacements delta. Consider
caps

    a.(p-z)+u.(X-y)>=-delta,       Gamma(u)=1.         (2)

For each p, classify its trace as full, empty, or proper. With
l_p(u)=min_(K_p)u.(X-y) and h_p(u)=max_(K_p)u.(X-y), these conditions are

    full:   a.(p-z)>=-delta-l_p(u),
    empty:  a.(p-z)<=-delta-h_p(u),
    proper: fix the actual scalar a.(p-z).

The proper scalar lies between the two displayed bounded thresholds. All
right sides are uniformly bounded for bounded delta and Gamma(u)=1. For each
of the finitely many status patterns, the constraint normals are fixed vectors
plus or minus (p-z); proper equalities are represented by both inequalities.
Choose a minimum-norm feasible replacement a'. The finite active-set/Farkas
bound proved in the sampled-majorant source bounds |a'| uniformly in these
right sides and in the status pattern. The original a is feasible, so no
existence issue arises.

The replacement preserves EVERY proper fiber cut and every full or empty
fiber mass, and hence the cap mass. A cut exactly on a supporting facet can
be put in the full or empty class appropriate to its volume: the boundary
facet has zero d-volume. Nonzero u prevents an entire positive fiber from
lying in the cap plane. Thus all closed-cap cases are included.

It follows, in particular, that the infimum of the masses (2) at a fixed
source and displacement is attained by a nonvertical cap. Take a minimizing
sequence, clamp its tilts uniformly, and pass to a compact subsequence in
(a',u). Cap volumes are continuous there, since the limiting continuous normal
is still nonzero. This lemma does not assert a uniform tilt bound as the real
source base itself varies; its fixed constraint matrix depends on z.

## 3. The convex signed radius and its exact atomic domain

Define the extended-valued signed function

    r_Q(z,y)=sup_(a,Gamma(u)=1)
                 [a.z+u.y-c_Q^-(a,u)].               (3)

It is convex and lower semicontinuous, being a supremum of finite affine
functions of (z,y). Its value is never minus infinity. Its exact finite domain
in the base coordinate is

    r_Q(z,y)<infinity iff b_base(z)>Q.                (4)

To prove finiteness, for any a let G={p:a.(p-z)>=0}. Its whole-fiber mass is
at least b_base(z)>Q. Put m(u)=min_(p,X in K_p)u.X. At threshold a.z+m(u),
the cap contains every fiber in G, so its mass is strictly above Q. Hence
c_Q^->a.z+m(u), and

    r_Q(z,y)<=max_(Gamma(u)=1)[u.y-m(u)]<infinity.

For the converse choose a closed atomic halfspace G through z of mass at most
Q. Its complement is nonempty because Q<M. The finite set of excluded bases
has a strictly negative margin: a_0.(p-z)<=-gamma<0. For large k, the cap with
base tilt k a_0 and threshold k a_0.z-k gamma/2 captures EXACTLY the full fibers
in G. Thus c_Q^-(k a_0,u) is no greater than this threshold, and the margin in
(3) tends to infinity. This includes b_base(z)=Q, not just strict inequality.

At every finite value the supremum in (3) is ATTAINED. Take a maximizing
sequence of left-quantile caps. Their margins r lie in a fixed bounded interval
by (4) and any one comparison normal. Each cap has mass Q and threshold
c=a.z+u.y-r. Apply Section2 with delta=r to preserve its mass and margin while
clamping a. A convergent subsequence gives a cap of mass Q with the limiting
maximal margin. Its new left quantile can only increase that margin; the
definition of the supremum forces equality. This proves attainment even when
the tail has a gap and without an own-section regularity assumption.

## 4. Exact scalar buffered-depth sublevel

For a real mark w=(z,y) in C and a nonnegative scalar displacement delta,
define B(w,delta) as the minimum of b_base(z) and the infimum of cap masses

    a.(Z-z)+u.(X-y)>=-delta,       Gamma(u)=1.

Then EXACTLY

    B(w,delta)<=Q iff delta<=r_Q(w).                  (5)

If b_base(z)<=Q, both assertions hold because r_Q=infinity. Otherwise the
nonvertical infimum is attained by Section2. Its mass is at most Q precisely
when a.z+u.y-delta>=c_Q^-(a,u), i.e. its margin is at least delta. Conversely,
if delta<=r_Q, use the attained maximizer from Section3. Thus equality in (5)
is an actual closed-cap certificate, not a supremum approached only at an
unbounded base tilt.

The signed radius matters at zero displacement. If r_Q<0, even delta=0 is
infeasible. If r_Q=0, delta=0 is feasible but every positive displacement is
infeasible. Taking a positive part is harmless only when the parameter being
bounded is strictly positive and the energy is positive.

At a SAMPLED interior mark with b_base(p)>Q and r_Q>=0, the maximizing cap in
(3) has a proper own trace. It contains the source, and a cap containing the
whole own fiber has mass at least b_base(p), by the audited whole-fiber
capture lemma. The proper trace makes the tail strictly decrease locally at
its Q-quantile. Consequently at such sampled marks the scalar threshold is
strict on the two sides: B(w,delta)<Q for 0<=delta<r_Q and B(w,r_Q)=Q. This
extra strictness is not imported at an unsampled real base.

## 5. The actual convex obstacle

Let E_(C_z)(y) be ordinary projective energy, with its continuous zero extension
to the fiber boundary, and set F(z,y)=E_(C_z)(y)^(1/d). The audited joint
Minkowski theorem makes F concave on the actual canonical body. Fix epsilon>0.
For a positive finite parameter value l, the buffer displacement is

    delta=epsilon [l E_(C_z)(y)/M]^(1/(d+1)).

On positive-energy marks define

    T_Q(z,y)=(M/epsilon^(d+1))
                    [max(r_Q(z,y),0)]^(d+1)/E_(C_z)(y).        (6)

Use T_Q=infinity when r_Q=infinity. On fiber-boundary marks use T_Q=infinity.
Then for EVERY positive l and actual real mark,

    B(w,epsilon[l E(w)/M]^(1/(d+1)))<=Q
                         iff l<=T_Q(w).              (7)

For E>0 this follows directly from (5), including r_Q<0 because then the
right side allows no positive l. The energy-zero boundary assertion follows
from the next paragraph. Formula (7) deliberately excludes l=0: at r_Q<0
its left side is false while the positive-part obstacle is zero.

At every fiber-boundary mark the original depth is zero, and r_Q>0 (or infinity).
Indeed choose a nonzero continuous supporting normal of C_z at y. Its support
height as a function of the real base is the finite LP roof of the sampled
heights h_(K_p)(u). That polyhedral concave roof has a finite affine majorant
touching at z. It yields an ambient supporting cap through w with nonzero
continuous normal and zero mixed mass. Since Q>0 and its tail is continuous,
its left Q-quantile is strictly below its support threshold, giving a positive
margin in (3). Energy zero leaves every finite buffer zero, so (7) is automatic
there. No division by zero is used in the proof.

The extended obstacle T_Q is CONVEX and lower semicontinuous on C. On F>0 this
is the convex perspective

    g(x,s)=x^(d+1)/s^d,       x>=0, s>0,

applied to the convex x=max(r_Q,0) and concave s=F. The perspective is increasing
in x and decreasing in s, so the standard two-step convexity inequality gives
the claim directly. Its closed extension has g(x,0)=infinity for x>0 and
 g(0,0)=0. At an actual fiber boundary r_Q>0, so this extension agrees with
the infinity convention in (6). Lower semicontinuity follows from the closed
perspective, the lower semicontinuity of r_Q, continuity of F, and the same
boundary positivity. One can set T_Q=infinity outside C if an ambient
extended-valued convex function is desired.

Therefore for a fixed body and any positive concave full-space weight L,
its maximum buffered depth on the actual sampled set is at most Q EXACTLY
when

    L(w)<=T_Q(w) for every sampled w in S.             (8)

This is an upper convex obstacle imposed on a concave function. Convexity of
the obstacle does not make (8) a proved payment theorem or identify which
finite subset of marked constraints suffices. In particular it does not
remove the archived volume-martingale domain obstruction.

## 6. A real-base plateau that distinguishes the archived threshold

Here is an actual complete binary-base example with a genuine positive
buffer plateau at an UNSAMPLED real source. Let d=1,

    P={(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)},
    c_00=c_10=c_01=0,  c_11=1,
    K_p=[c_p-h,c_p+h],       0<h<1/4.

These vertex fibers are exactly the corresponding fibers of their canonical
convex hull. Each has mass 2h, so M=8h. At the real source

    z=(1/2,1/2),  y=1/4,

its actual fiber is [-h,1/2+h], and its atomic depth is 4h. Choose Q=2h and
Gamma(u)=|u|. For u=1, the four centered vertex margins are

    m_00=-(a_1+a_2)/2-1/4,
    m_10=(a_1-a_2)/2-1/4,
    m_01=(-a_1+a_2)/2-1/4,
    m_11=(a_1+a_2)/2+3/4.

The identities m_00+m_11=1/2 and m_10+m_01=-1/2 show that some margin is at
least 1/4. For u=-1 the roles of these pairs reverse, giving the same lower
bound. Thus every cap with delta>=0 captures one whole interval and has mass
at least Q. With a=0,u=1, it captures only the (1,1) interval for

    0<=delta<=1/4-h.

Therefore the actual depth equals Q throughout this nontrivial buffer range.
Moreover any cap of mass at most Q must have exactly one wholly captured
interval and no positive mass from the other three. In the negative-sum pair,
both intervals must be among those other three: the positive-sum pair already
contains a wholly captured interval, so a wholly captured interval outside
that pair would exceed Q. One of the negative-pair margins is at least -1/4;
hence delta<=1/4-h. It follows
that the signed radius in (3) is exactly 1/4-h.

For the displayed a=0,u=1 cap the Q-plateau in threshold space is [h,1-h].
Its LEFT endpoint gives the positive margin 1/4-h; its RIGHT endpoint gives
-3/4+h. The archived nonnegative right-quantile radius has value zero at this
mark, because unbuffered depth already reaches Q. Its superlevel threshold is
zero, whereas the present positive sublevel obstacle is strictly positive:

    E_(C_z)(y)=1/2+2h,
    T_Q(z,y)=(8h/epsilon^2)(1/4-h)^2/(1/2+2h).

This is not a contradiction: the two thresholds describe opposite closed
inequalities, and an unsampled-base plateau satisfies both over a range.
At all sampled binary vertices the atomic depth itself equals Q, so their
sublevel obstacle is infinity as required by (4). The example proves no
counterexample to a mixed centerpoint statement.

## 7. Exact scope of the new formulation

The archive already contains the right-quantile projected superlevel epigraph.
The present additions are the left-quantile closed sublevel obstacle, its
strict atomic-domain convention, finite status-clamping attainment, and the
real-base plateau calibration. All ambient oblique directions remain in (3).
No cap-count estimate, finite-dimensional replacement of the obstacle, or
Gamma inequality is inferred merely from its convexity.

The companion `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_left_quantile_obstacle_slab_recovery.py` passes
120,489 exact checks of the actual interval clipping calibration, the two
quantile endpoints, and the perspective Hessian's nonnegative rank-one form.
Its finite tilt grids supplement the all-normal pair-sum proof in Section 6;
they are not used as a substitute for that proof or for status-clamping.
